newsitem.title: UK: UK right to argue ERM not requisite to EMU-Davies.
newsitem.headline: UK right to argue ERM not requisite to EMU-Davies.

text.p: Britain is right to argue that membership of the EU's exchange rate mechanism is not a necessary pre-requisite for European monetary union (EMU), Gavyn Davies, managing director and chief international economist at Goldman Sachs said on Wednesday.
Asked by Reuters if he though Britain could join EMU without prior ERM membership, Davies said: "I don't think you can say for sure what the answer is."

"My reading of the treaty suggests that the intention of the drafters was clearly that narrow-band entry to the ERM should exist for two years prior to membership. But the narrow bands don't exist any more, so I can certainly see that it is arguable, or what Britain is arguing is right," Davies told Reuters on the fringes of Goldman Sachs' foreign exchange conference.

"What looked very clear when the treaty was drafted, no longer applies because the bands that the treaty referred to no longer exist. That will have to be debated and can only be determined by the European Council of Ministers," he added.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, however, has said that there is no question of waiving the Maastricht Treaty rule that a currency must be part of the ERM for two years to make it eligible for the single currency.
He reaffirmed that point at a meeting of EU finance ministers last week, the first one attended by Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
But at the same meeting, Brown told reporters the two-year rule was not set in stone. Asked if the pound would have to rejoin the ERM to allow British entry into EMU, Brown replied simply: "No."

Davies, a long-time adviser to the Labour party which ousted the ruling Conservatives on May 1, said on Wednesday it would be dangerous for Britain to rejoin the EU's exchange rate mechanism at the moment.
"To join would be a very risky thing," Davies said.
Davies is widely tipped to be appointed to a deputy governorship at the Bank of England.
He said that if the UK joined, joining the ERM at a central rate of 2.50 to 2.60 marks, with 15 percent bands, would capture all the movement in sterling over the past six years.
"Anything above 2.60 or below 2.40 marks would be problematic," he told Reuters.

But achieving such a level would be hard: "First of all, getting a 2.50 exchange rate agreed with the rest of Europe and then keeping it within implied narrow bands (around 2.50) would be tricky," he said.
